power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

However, there remains little research with population-based samples across childhood. We report on additional problems, as measured by the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, in a population-based sample of 135 twins with ASD, 55 non-ASD co-twins, and 144 comparison twins low in ASD traits. This temperamental predisposition is characterized by heightened environmental sensitivity. The current prospective longitudinal study examined whether BI at 15 months of age predicted lower CU-traits across development to age 21. A longitudinal sample of normatively developing children (n = 125) was used. BI was assessed at 15 months using a standard stranger/robot paradigm. CU-traits were assessed at 2, 5, 9, 12, 14, 17, and 21 years with parent, teacher, and self-reports. Developmental pathways across all available data points were examined using Bayesian mixed models and k-means cluster analysis. "Callous-unemotional (CU) traits predict behavioral problems in adolescence. But little is known about early modulatory factors. Behavioral Inhibition (BI) in particular has been suggested to protect against the development of CU-traits. This temperamental predisposition is characterized by heightened environmental sensitivity. The current prospective longitudinal study examined whether BI at 15 months of age predicted lower CU-traits across development to age 21. A longitudinal sample of normatively developing children (n = 125) was used. BI was assessed at 15 months using a standard stranger/robot paradigm. CU-traits were assessed at 2, 5, 9, 12, 14, 17, and 21 years with parent, teacher, and self-reports. Developmental pathways across all available data points were examined using Bayesian mixed models and k-means cluster analysis. Infant BI predicted lower CU-traits across development for girls, suggesting that BI buffers the long-term development of CU-traits for girls. CU-traits peaked in early adulthood. Boys scored higher and showed higher increases in CU-traits than girls from childhood onward. There was no gender difference regarding infant BI. Together, the findings demonstrated gender differences in the development of CU-traits, with a protective role of BI for girls. These results shed new light on the developmental trajectories and protective factors of CU-traits and provide starting points for interventions aiming at increasing children’s responsiveness to external cues to prevent antisocial traits and conduct problems. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2022 APA, all rights reserved)",

"Background: While it has been purported that excessive screen time can lead to behavioral problems, it has also been suggested that children with behavioral dysregulation receive more access to screens to manage problematic behavior. In this study, both temporally stable and longitudinal associations between screen time and externalizing and internalizing behaviors across childhood are examined to directly address this issue of directionality. Methods: Data are from a prospective cohort of 10,172 Irish children, collected between 2010 and 2018 when children were ages 3, 5, 7, and 9. Children’s screen time (hours/day) and externalizing and internalizing behaviors (Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire) were assessed via caregiver report. Random‐intercepts cross‐lagged panel models were used to estimate longitudinal bidirectional associations while controlling for temporally stable (i.e., ‘time‐invariant’ or ‘trait‐like’) differences between children. Results: Temporally stable differences between children were observed for both screen time and behavior problems. Longitudinal trajectories for screen time lacked stability; however, and externalizing and internalizing behaviors stabilized increasingly during later childhood. Greater externalizing and internalizing behaviors at age 3 were directionally associated with increased screen time at age 5. "The association between psychopathic traits and conduct problems has been extensively analyzed, with results showing a significant predictive effect of psychopathic traits on later conduct problems. However, some recent research has evidenced some reversed effects, with early-onset conduct problems also showing a significant effect on psychopathic traits. The present study aimed to examine the longitudinal effects (i.e., autoregressive, direct, and bidirectional) between the three psychopathy dimensions (i.e., interpersonal, affective, and behavioral), and conduct problems in two data collections spanning one year (T1-T2). The potential mediation effect from inconsistent parenting and parental warmth was also analyzed. Data were collected, trough parents’ reports, in a sample of 1.833 children (48.8% girls; Mage = 4.24; SD = 0.92), participating in the ELISA study (Longitudinal Study for a Healthy Childhood). A cross-lagged path analysis with mediation effects was performed in Mplus. Results showed autoregressive, direct and bidirectional effects between psychopathic traits and conduct problems. Hence, whilst T1 conduct problems predicted all psychopathy dimensions in T2, only callous-unemotional and impulsive/need of stimulation traits measured in T1 predicted conduct problems in T2. Finally, some marginal mediation effects from inconsistent parenting and parental warmth were also observed, particularly in the relationship between interpersonal and affective psychopathic traits, and later CP through parental warmth. Current findings provide relevant implications for developmental models of psychopathic traits, as well as for predictive models and preventive strategies on early-onset conduct problems. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2022 APA, all rights reserved)",

"Objectives: Although there is some evidence on the longitudinal associations between bullying perpetration and narcissistic personality traits, their joint developmental trajectories across early to late adolescence are largely unknown. Accordingly, we examined the co-development of bullying perpetration and narcissistic personality traits across adolescence and examined the childhood predictors of these joint trajectories. Method: Self-reports of bullying and narcissistic personality traits were assessed across 6 years of adolescence from Grade 7 (i.e., age 13) to Grade 12 (i.e., age 18) in a sample of 616 Canadian adolescents and childhood predictors were assessed in Grades 5 and 6. Results: As predicted, latent class growth analyses demonstrated that most adolescents were reflected in a trajectory of low decreasing bullying (82.0%) and a smaller group followed a moderate stable trajectory of bullying (18.0%). The majority of adolescents followed a moderate stable trajectory of narcissistic traits (56.3%), followed by a high increasing trajectory of narcissistic traits (22.8%), and a low decreasing trajectory of narcissistic traits (20.9%). Six percent of adolescents followed a high-risk dual trajectory of moderate stable bullying and high increasing narcissistic traits (high-risk group). Also as predicted, higher hyperactivity, higher frustration, and lower anxiety in childhood differentiated the high-risk group from a low-risk group (low decreasing bullying and low decreasing narcissistic traits; 19.0%). Higher childhood hyperactivity also differentiated a group of adolescents who followed a trajectory of moderate stable bullying and moderate stable narcissistic traits (10.0%) from the low-risk group. Results showed that moderate stable bullying was a better indicator of high increasing and moderate stable trajectories of narcissistic personality traits than the reverse. Conclusions: Findings suggest adolescence is a time when personality and bullying reflect dynamic and heterogeneous development. Early intervention of childhood risk factors may help prevent a high-risk developmental course of bullying and narcissistic personality traits across adolescence. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2022 APA, all rights reserved)",

"Purpose: The behavioral disinhibition model (BDM) posits that a liability toward impulsivity evident by early adolescence underlies the coemergence of antisocial behavior and alcohol use (i.e., problem behaviors) in early-adolescence to mid-adolescence, but that the subsequent development of these problem behaviors (rather than impulsivity itself) predicts the emergence of antisocial personality disorder (APD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD) in late adolescence. The present study was designed to test these predictions of the BDM from early to late adolescence. Methods: We used five-year longitudinal self-report data from the Philadelphia Trajectory Study that was collected from 2006–2012. Mediational analyses were performed using the Random Intercept Cross-lagged Panel Model, which enables the detection of within-person predictions of changes in problem behaviors during adolescence. The sample was ethnically and socioeconomically diverse, including 364 urban US community youth (at baseline: Mage = 13.51(.95); 49.1% female). Results: Consistent with the BDM, mediational analyses revealed that changes in early adolescent impulsivity predicted late adolescent APD and AUD criteria, mediated by changes in mid-adolescent alcohol use and conduct problems. Discussion: Interventions targeting impulsivity in early adolescence could potentially halt the cascading chain of events leading to both late adolescent APD and AUD by decelerating growth in antisocial behavior and alcohol use during early-adolescence to mid-adolescence. From mid-adolescence to late-adolescence, the consequences of early impulsivity, especially involvement in antisocial behaviors, become a more relevant predictor of both APD and AUD rather than impulsivity itself. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2023 APA, all rights reserved)",

"The present study integrates coping research into a current model of alcohol use disorders etiology, with the goal of better articulating the development of alcohol use disorders. Research has shown that an emotional and impulsive temperament may predispose a person to later risky drinking, and further that much of this risk is due to an increased likelihood of learning that alcohol is an effective means of reducing negative emotions (termed coping expectancies). The Acquired Preparedness (AP; Anderson & Smith, 2001) model formalizes this idea into a testable mediational model; however, the mechanisms which connect personality to the development of coping expectancies is not well-understood. Aim 1 of the was to extend the AP model to include coping constructs, particularly avoidant coping, providing an important test of the longitudinal mechanisms by which early-appearing temperament characteristics convey risk for outcomes in adulthood. Aim 2 of the current dissertation was to understand the relations of avoidant coping to the development of coping expectancies. I hypothesized that 1) avoidant coping would predict coping expectancies, and that avoidant coping would be preceded by emotionality and impulsivity. I further hypothesized that 2) avoidant coping would predict trajectories of coping expectancies, and 3) individuals who have the most opportunities to learn the affect regulation function of alcohol – through their own drinking and through seeing peers drink – will have the strongest link between avoidant coping and coping expectancies.I tested these hypotheses in a large longitudinal dataset (n=454) following adolescents from age 13 into their 30s. The Adult and Family Development Project (AFDP, PI: Chassin) was a comprehensive longitudinal evaluation of individual, contextual, and familial factors related to the development of alcohol use and beliefs. Approximately half of the children in the sample lived with a parent with a history of alcohol use disorder at the time of the first assessment. "Background: Insomnia is prevalent among children and adolescents and is associated with a wide range of negative outcomes. Knowledge about its determinants is therefore important, but due to the lack of longitudinal studies, such knowledge is limited. The aim of the present inquiry is to identify child and family predictors of future pediatric insomnia within a psycho-bio-behavioral framework. Methods: A representative community sample (n = 1,037) was followed biennially from 4 to 14 years of age (2007–2017). Insomnia was defined based on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV) criteria and was diagnosed by a semistructured clinical interview of children (from age eight years of age) and parents (all ages). Predictors included parent ratings of child emotional reactivity, family functioning, and marital conflict; self-reports of personality; and teacher-rated emotion regulation skills. Results: Random intercept cross-lagged analyses revealed that within-person increases (ie, relative to the child's typical levels across childhood) in emotional reactivity and decreases in emotion regulation skills predicted insomnia diagnosis two years later from ages 4 to 14 after adjusting for previous insomnia and all unmeasured time-invariant factors. Previous insomnia was the strongest predictor of later insomnia, whereas family functioning and marital conflict did not predict insomnia. Conclusions: Increases in emotional reactivity and decreases in emotion regulation skills predicted insomnia above and beyond all unmeasured time-invariant factors and could be targets for interventions. Previous insomnia predicted later insomnia, thereby underscoring the importance of detecting, preventing, and treating insomnia at an early age. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2022 APA, all rights reserved)",

"Background: Parent-child relationship quality (PCRQ) and parental monitoring (PM) are associated with adolescent behavior problems following child maltreatment (CM). Whether these associations are best characterized as between (trait) or within-person (state) differences is unknown. Objective: Disaggregate between and within-person effects for PCRQ and PM on adolescent behavior problems and test whether these effects vary as a function of prior CM. Participants and setting: Participants (n = 941) are from the Longitudinal Studies on Child Abuse and Neglect (LONGSCAN). Methods: Multi-level modeling was employed using PCRQ, PM, and adolescent behaviors assessed at ages 12, 14, and 16 and confirmed CM prior to age 12. Results: At the between-person level, adolescents with higher average levels of PCRQ and PM had significantly lower initial levels of externalizing (b = −9.47 and −5.54, respectively, p's < 0.05; possible range 0–66) and internalizing behaviors (b = −4.45 and −6.41, respectively, p's < 0.001; possible range 0–62). At the within-person level, greater declines in externalizing and internalizing behaviors were found when individuals reported higher-than-usual levels of PCRQ (b = −4.99 and −2.59, respectively, for externalizing and internalizing, p's < 0.001) and PM (b = −3.58 and −1.69, respectively, for externalizing and internalizing, p's < 0.001). There was an interaction between PM and CM on internalizing behaviors over time (b = −1.15, p = 0.026). Conclusions: There are between and within-person effects of PCRQ and PM on adolescent behavior problems. Adolescents with CM histories and low levels of PM may be at risk for sustained internalizing behaviors. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2023 APA, all rights reserved)",

"The longitudinal study examined whether and how children’s temperament traits in particular but also their age, sex as well as maternal education and age predict maternal socialization values. The sample was drawn from the IDEFICS study and included 567 mothers from Estonia whose children were 2–9 years old at Time 0 and 4–11 years old at Time 1. The findings showed that children’s temperament at Time 0 predicted maternal socialization values at Time 1, but not vice versa. Mothers who perceived their child to be more imaginative at Time 0 considered self‐maximization socialization values more important and social conformity‐related values less important at Time 1. Child’s conscientiousness and extraversion were linked positively to social conformity‐related socialization values. Older mothers and those with higher level of education put more emphasis on self‐maximization socialization values. Children’s age and sex were not related to socialization values. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2021 APA, all rights reserved)",

"Temperament is related to cognition, but it is unclear whether reciprocal associations exist with early developmental trajectories. Children from the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (N = 8,677) were assessed over four waves on verbal ability at ages 8/9, nonverbal ability at ages 8/9 and 10/11, and parent-rated temperament every two years from ages 8/9 to 14/15. Latent difference score analyses indicated correlated changes between ages 8/9 and 10/11. Increased nonverbal ability over the first two years was associated with declined reactivity and increased persistence. Latent growth curve models further indicated that nonverbal and verbal ability at baseline were associated with declined reactivity and increased persistence over the six years. These findings suggest bidirectional associations between childhood cognitive ability and temperament development. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2023 APA, all rights reserved)",

"Background: Psychiatric symptoms are commonly comorbid in childhood. The ability to disentangle unique and shared correlates of comorbid symptoms facilitates personalized medicine. Cognitive control is implicated broadly in psychopathology, including in pediatric disorders characterized by anxiety and irritability. To disentangle cognitive control correlates of anxiety versus irritability, the current study leveraged both cross-sectional and longitudinal data from early childhood into adolescence. Methods: For this study, 89 participants were recruited from a large longitudinal research study on early-life temperament to investigate associations of developmental trajectories of anxiety and irritability symptoms (from ages 2 to 15) as well as associations of anxiety and irritability symptoms measured cross-sectionally at age 15 with neural substrates of conflict and error processing assessed at age 15 using the flanker task. Results: Results of whole-brain multivariate linear models revealed that anxiety at age 15 was uniquely associated with decreased neural response to conflict across multiple regions implicated in attentional control and conflict adaptation. Conversely, irritability at age 15 was uniquely associated with increased neural response to conflict in regions implicated in response inhibition. Developmental trajectories of anxiety and irritability interacted in relation to neural responses to both error and conflict. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that neural correlates of conflict processing may relate uniquely to anxiety and irritability. Continued cross-symptom research on the neural correlates of cognitive control could stimulate advances in individualized treatment for anxiety and irritability during child and adolescent development. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2023 APA, all rights reserved)",

"The reactivity-regulation model suggests that the origins and maintenance of shyness results from relatively high levels of reactivity in combination with relatively low levels of regulation. Although this model has received some empirical support, there are still issues regarding directionality of the relations among variables and a dearth of studies examining the joint influence of reactivity and regulation on the prospective development of shyness. Using a longitudinal design, we first examined whether the relations among reactivity, regulation, and shyness were unidirectional or bidirectional in a sample of 1284 children (49.8% female, 84.1% White; mean parental education fell between associate degree/diploma and undergraduate degree) assessed annually across three waves from late childhood and early adolescence (Mage = 10.72 years) to adolescence (Mage = 12.42 years) and then examined whether reactivity and regulation interacted to influence the development of shyness over time. At Wave 1, shyness was related to higher levels of reactivity and lower levels of regulation at Wave 2, but neither reactivity nor regulation at Wave 1 predicted shyness at Wave 2. At Wave 2, shyness predicted greater reactivity at Wave 3, but shyness at Wave 3 was only predicted by lower levels of regulation at Wave 2. Contrary to the reactivity-regulation model of shyness, we found that relatively high levels of reactivity and low levels of regulation predicted a steep decrease in shyness over 3 years. These results are discussed in the context of the socioemotional difficulties experienced by shy individuals and demonstrate the importance of empirically evaluating long-standing models of personality development. Using a longitudinal design, we first examined whether the relations among reactivity, regulation, and shyness were unidirectional or bidirectional in a sample of 1284 children (49.8% female, 84.1% White; mean parental education fell between associate degree/diploma and undergraduate degree) assessed annually across three waves from late childhood and early adolescence (Mage = 10.72 years) to adolescence (Mage = 12.42 years) and then examined whether reactivity and regulation interacted to influence the development of shyness over time. At Wave 1, shyness was related to higher levels of reactivity and lower levels of regulation at Wave 2, but neither reactivity nor regulation at Wave 1 predicted shyness at Wave 2. At Wave 2, shyness predicted greater reactivity at Wave 3, but shyness at Wave 3 was only predicted by lower levels of regulation at Wave 2. Contrary to the reactivity-regulation model of shyness, we found that relatively high levels of reactivity and low levels of regulation predicted a steep decrease in shyness over 3 years. These results are discussed in the context of the socioemotional difficulties experienced by shy individuals and demonstrate the importance of empirically evaluating long-standing models of personality development. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2021 APA, all rights reserved)",

"Developmental patterns of personality pathology traits are not well delineated from childhood through late adolescence. In the present study, participants (N = 675, 56% female) were recruited to create three cohorts of third (n = 205), sixth (n = 248), and ninth (n = 222) graders to form an accelerated longitudinal cohort design. We assessed six PD (avoidant, dependent, histrionic, narcissistic, borderline, schizotypal) traits based on DSM-IV trait diagnostic conceptualizations via parent report at baseline, 18 months, and 36 months. According to parent report, mean levels of avoidant, dependent, histrionic, narcissistic, borderline, and schizotypal traits all declined for both boys and girls. The changes in dependent and histrionic traits were of medium effect size, and the changes in avoidant, narcissistic, borderline, and schizotypal traits were of small effect size. Over the 3 years of the study, the traits of each PD also demonstrated moderate to high rank-order stability. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2021 APA, all rights reserved)",

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 396 columns across 9 data files.
#### Issues Identified

30 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 9 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 9 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  1 of 9 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  16 installable dependencies detected.
- 289 statistics stored from the extracted output; 3 of 43 reported tests matched (7%).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 9 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:9, File = c("01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R", 
"02 SplineApproach_Agreeableness.R", "Supplement_v2.R", "Supplement_v2.Rmd", 
"03 SplineApproach_Conscientiousness.R", "04 SplineApproach_Extraversion.R", 
"05 SplineApproach_Neuroticism.R", "06 SplineApproach_Openness.R", 
"07 SplineApproach_BigFiveOnly.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", "01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R", 
"01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R", "01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R", 
"01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R", "01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R", 
"01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R", "01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R", 
"01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R"), Basis = c("numeric", "dependency", 
"dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency", 
"dependency", "dependency")), row.names = c(NA, -9L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**3 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `effect_19_DataID.csv` to `Data/effect_19_DataID.csv` (in 01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R); `data_new_update.xlsx` to `Data/data_new_update.xlsx` (in 01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R); `Moderator_Coding_Roberts.xlsx` to `Data/Moderator_Coding_Roberts.xlsx` (in 01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 3 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `spline_approach_all.rdata`, `table_descriptives_edited.xlsx`, `spline_approach_big5.rdata`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 9 scripts: 1 ran without error, 2 errored, 6 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **7 scripts stopped on a file another script writes**, so they were run once more after the other scripts: `02 SplineApproach_Agreeableness.R` (data_ma.RData, V_all.RData); `Supplement_v2.Rmd` (data_ma.RData, V_all.RData); `03 SplineApproach_Conscientiousness.R` (data_ma.RData, V_all.RData); `04 SplineApproach_Extraversion.R` (data_ma.RData, V_all.RData); `05 SplineApproach_Neuroticism.R` (data_ma.RData, V_all.RData); `06 SplineApproach_Openness.R` (data_ma.RData, V_all.RData); `07 SplineApproach_BigFiveOnly.R` (data_BigFiveOnly.RData, V_BigFiveOnly.RData). 6 files were written in another folder than where the script looked, so before that run we copied them there: `data_ma.RData` to `Scripts/data_ma.RData` for `02 SplineApproach_Agreeableness.R`; `data_ma.RData` to `Data/Prepared/data_ma.RData` for `Supplement_v2.Rmd`; `data_BigFiveOnly.RData` to `Scripts/data_BigFiveOnly.RData` for `07 SplineApproach_BigFiveOnly.R`; `V_all.RData` to `Scripts/V_all.RData` for `02 SplineApproach_Agreeableness.R`; `V_all.RData` to `Data/Prepared/V_all.RData` for `Supplement_v2.Rmd`; `V_BigFiveOnly.RData` to `Scripts/V_BigFiveOnly.RData` for `07 SplineApproach_BigFiveOnly.R`. The scripts assume they all run from one folder; saying which, or building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), solves this. Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). 

*a script hit a `could not find function "..."` error; we added the `library()` calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R", 
"02 SplineApproach_Agreeableness.R", "Supplement_v2.R", "Supplement_v2.Rmd", 
"03 SplineApproach_Conscientiousness.R", "04 SplineApproach_Extraversion.R", 
"05 SplineApproach_Neuroticism.R", "06 SplineApproach_Openness.R", 
"07 SplineApproach_BigFiveOnly.R"), Outcome = c("ran_ok", "timed_out", 
"errored", "errored", "timed_out", "timed_out", "timed_out", 
"timed_out", "timed_out"), Detail = c("", "timeout", "undefined_variable", 
"runtime", "timeout", "timeout", "timeout", "timeout", "timeout"
), "Time (s)" = c(47.2, 300.3, 4.4, 4.3, 300.3, 300.3, 300.3, 
300.4, 300.3)), row.names = c(NA, -9L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Supplement_v2.R", "Missing variable" = "studies", 
    "Defined in" = "(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**8 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: 01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Supplement_v2.Rmd", "03 SplineApproach_Conscientiousness.R", 
"06 SplineApproach_Openness.R", "04 SplineApproach_Extraversion.R", 
"01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R", "05 SplineApproach_Neuroticism.R", 
"02 SplineApproach_Agreeableness.R", "07 SplineApproach_BigFiveOnly.R"
), "setwd() removed" = c(1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 4L, 2L, 2L, 6L), "Path(s) it set" = c("/Users/phaehn/switchdrive/Post-Doc/Forschungsprojekte/18 Meta-Analysis Individual Differences of Personality Traits Across the Lifespan/Analyses", 
"(non-literal)", "(non-literal)", "(non-literal)", "(non-literal)", 
"(non-literal)", "(non-literal)", "(non-literal)")), row.names = c(NA, 
-8L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`library()` calls added**

**1 script uses functions from packages it does not load itself.** The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. To run it we added the `library()` calls below at the top. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after adding `library()` calls it should make itself**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Supplement_v2.R", "library() calls added" = "library(papaja), library(tidyverse), library(readxl), library(kableExtra), library(cowplot), library(psych), library(metafor), library(ggiraph), library(combinat), library(metaforest), library(RcppAlgos), library(writexl), library(questionr)"), row.names = "Supplement_v2.R", class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

text.text: This meta-analysis was preregistered at https://osf.io/w7fhd.
text.formatted: This meta-analysis was preregistered at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/w7fhd">https://osf.io/w7fhd</ref>.

text.text: The meta-analytic dataset, coding material, R scripts, and a HTML document with supplementary findings can be retrieved from https://osf.io/qdnyk.
text.formatted: The meta-analytic dataset, coding material, R scripts, and a HTML document with supplementary findings can be retrieved from <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/qdnyk">https://osf.io/qdnyk</ref>.

text.text: We would like to thank Leyla Rosero Betancourt for her support with the literature search and coding of studies for this meta-analysis.
Furthermore, we would like to thank Ted Schwaba, Anqing Zheng, Christopher J.
Personality trait variance captures how much people differ from each other in their patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors.

This meta-analysis shows that the variance of personality traits remains largely stable across the lifespan, meaning that people do not become systematically more similar or more different from one another as they age.
Thus, personality traits can be used to describe and explain differences between people across the entire lifespan.
Does the Variance of Personality Traits Change Across the Lifespan?
text.formatted: <head>Does the Variance of Personality Traits Change Across the Lifespan?

text.text: A Meta-Analytic
text.formatted: A Meta-Analytic</head>

text.text: Personality traits are relatively stable patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors (Allport, 1961).
text.formatted: Personality traits are relatively stable patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors <ref type="bibr">(Allport, 1961)</ref>.

text.text: Although being more stable than other constructs, there is now compelling evidence that the mean levels of personality traits change across the entire lifespan, suggesting that, on average, people experience age-graded increases or decreases in trait levels over time (Anusic & Schimmack, 2016; Bleidorn et al., 2022; Haehner, Krämer, Schaefer, et al., 2025; Seifert et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Although being more stable than other constructs, there is now compelling evidence that the mean levels of personality traits change across the entire lifespan, suggesting that, on average, people experience age-graded increases or decreases in trait levels over time <ref type="bibr">(Anusic & Schimmack, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bleidorn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Krämer, Schaefer, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Seifert et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For example, the mean level of conscientiousness has been found to increase during young adulthood, peak around age 40 to 50, and then decrease again throughout the remainder of the lifespan (Bleidorn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: For example, the mean level of conscientiousness has been found to increase during young adulthood, peak around age 40 to 50, and then decrease again throughout the remainder of the lifespan <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast to the accumulating knowledge about lifespan changes in mean levels of personality traits, we know only little about changes in the variance of personality traits (Mõttus et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In contrast to the accumulating knowledge about lifespan changes in mean levels of personality traits, we know only little about changes in the variance of personality traits <ref type="bibr">(Mõttus et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The variance of personality traits captures the extent of individual differences in a population and may be considered as one of the core research targets of personality psychology (Allport, 1961).
text.formatted: The variance of personality traits captures the extent of individual differences in a population and may be considered as one of the core research targets of personality psychology <ref type="bibr">(Allport, 1961)</ref>.

text.text: Just as the mean-levels of personality traits change over the lifespan, the variance may do so as well (Nakagawa et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Just as the mean-levels of personality traits change over the lifespan, the variance may do so as well <ref type="bibr">(Nakagawa et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: A decrease in the variance of personality traits across the lifespan would, for instance, indicate that people become more alike as they age, whereas an increase would indicate that individual differences in personality traits become more pronounced.

Although numerous longitudinal studies provide descriptive information about variance changes of personality traits (e.g., Allemand et al., 2007; Borghuis et al., 2017; Haehner et al., 2023; Small et al., 2003), meta-analytic evidence on how the variance of personality traits changes across the lifespan is currently missing.
text.formatted: Although numerous longitudinal studies provide descriptive information about variance changes of personality traits (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Allemand et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Borghuis et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Small et al., 2003)</ref>, meta-analytic evidence on how the variance of personality traits changes across the lifespan is currently missing.

text.text: This is surprising given the empirical, theoretical, and practical relevance of this research question.

Specifically, a first reason to study changes in personality trait variance across the lifespan is that a trait's mean-level and variance can follow distinct trajectories over time (Nakagawa et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Specifically, a first reason to study changes in personality trait variance across the lifespan is that a trait's mean-level and variance can follow distinct trajectories over time <ref type="bibr">(Nakagawa et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Examining when and how the variance of personality traits changes across the lifespan thus offers a unique perspective on personality trait development beyond the examination of mean-level changes (Mõttus et al., 2016 (Mõttus et al., , 2017)).
text.formatted: Examining when and how the variance of personality traits changes across the lifespan thus offers a unique perspective on personality trait development beyond the examination of mean-level changes <ref type="bibr">(Mõttus et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Mõttus et al., , 2017))</ref>.

text.text: Second, contemporary personality development theories are ambiguous regarding their implications for whether and how the variance of personality traits changes across the lifespan (Caspi et al., 2005; McCrae & Costa, 2008; Roberts & Nickel, 2017; Specht et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Second, contemporary personality development theories are ambiguous regarding their implications for whether and how the variance of personality traits changes across the lifespan <ref type="bibr">(Caspi et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">McCrae & Costa, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & Nickel, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Specht et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, providing a robust empirical description of variance trajectories of personality traits could advance theories on personality development (Bleidorn, 2024; Mõttus et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Thus, providing a robust empirical description of variance trajectories of personality traits could advance theories on personality development <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bleidorn, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mõttus et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Third, investigating how the variance of personality traits changes across the lifespan is practically relevant, as the variance of a construct contextualizes observed patterns of mean-level change and determines its utility for predicting important life outcomes (Mõttus et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Third, investigating how the variance of personality traits changes across the lifespan is practically relevant, as the variance of a construct contextualizes observed patterns of mean-level change and determines its utility for predicting important life outcomes <ref type="bibr">(Mõttus et al., 2016</ref>).

text.text: If, for example, the variance of personality traits strongly decreases across the lifespan, personality traits might become less suitable to predict life outcomes in older ages, because the predictive power of a variable partly depends on its variability.
With the present meta-analysis, we aimed to provide a more comprehensive picture of the trajectory of personality trait variance across the lifespan.
We addressed two research questions: (1) How does the variance of personality traits (i.e., individual differences) develop across time and age?
(2) Are there methodological moderators of changes in the variance of personality traits?

Once a niche topic, the question of whether and how personality traits change across the lifespan has gained considerable research interest over the last three decades (e.g., Bleidorn et al., 2020 Bleidorn et al., , 2021 Bleidorn et al., , 2022;; Borghuis et al., 2017; R. I. Damian et al., 2019; Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2025; Roberts, Walton, & Viechtbauer, 2006; Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000).
text.formatted: Once a niche topic, the question of whether and how personality traits change across the lifespan has gained considerable research interest over the last three decades (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bleidorn et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bleidorn et al., , 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bleidorn et al., , 2022;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Borghuis et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">R. I. Damian et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts, Walton, & Viechtbauer, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Most of this research has focused on changes in the Big Five personality traits: agreeableness (being compassionate and forgiving), conscientiousness (being efficient and thorough), extraversion (being outgoing and energetic), neuroticism (being irritable and moody), and openness to experiences (being curious and unconventional; Soto & John, 2017).
text.formatted: Most of this research has focused on changes in the Big Five personality traits: agreeableness (being compassionate and forgiving), conscientiousness (being efficient and thorough), extraversion (being outgoing and energetic), neuroticism (being irritable and moody), and openness to experiences <ref type="bibr">(being curious and unconventional;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Soto & John, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Two indicators of personality trait changes have frequently been considered in studies and meta-analyses on personality development: (a) mean-level changes and (b) rank-order changes (Bleidorn et al., 2021; Borghuis et al., 2017; Haehner et al., 2022; Seifert et al., 2024; A. J. Wright et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Two indicators of personality trait changes have frequently been considered in studies and meta-analyses on personality development: (a) mean-level changes and (b) rank-order changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bleidorn et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Borghuis et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Seifert et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">A. J. Wright et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Mean-level changes describe the direction and extent of changes in the average level of personality traits.
Overall, the largest mean-level changes appear to occur in young adulthood; however, the Big Five traits differ in their individual mean-level trajectories.
For example, the mean-levels of extraversion have been found to decrease from young adulthood onward, whereas mean-levels of agreeableness increase until age 20 and then remain relatively stable.
Moreover, mean-level changes tend to be more pronounced over longer versus shorter retest intervals (Bleidorn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Moreover, mean-level changes tend to be more pronounced over longer versus shorter retest intervals <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Rank-order changes capture changes in the relative rank-ordering of people on traits within a population over time.

As summarized in a recent meta-analysis by Bleidorn et al. (2022), the rank-order stability of personality traits increases during adolescence before reaching a plateau in young adulthood, indicating that people become more consistent in their personality traits across the lifespan.
text.formatted: As summarized in a recent meta-analysis by <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bleidorn et al. (2022)</ref>, the rank-order stability of personality traits increases during adolescence before reaching a plateau in young adulthood, indicating that people become more consistent in their personality traits across the lifespan.

text.text: Furthermore, changes in rank-orders significantly increase over longer time intervals between assessments, with similar developmental patterns among all Big Five traits.

Understanding whether, when, and how personality traits change over time is of critical practical relevance because personality traits have been found to predict various important life outcomes, including well-being, health, relationship satisfaction, and workrelated success (Beck & Jackson, 2022; Bleidorn et al., 2019; Haehner, Shirima, et al., 2025; Soto, 2019).
text.formatted: Understanding whether, when, and how personality traits change over time is of critical practical relevance because personality traits have been found to predict various important life outcomes, including well-being, health, relationship satisfaction, and workrelated success <ref type="bibr">(Beck & Jackson, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bleidorn et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Shirima, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Soto, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Increases in neuroticism have, for example, been linked to the onset of mental and physical disorders and a declining health status (Jokela et al., 2018; A. J. Wright & Jackson, 2023).
text.formatted: Increases in neuroticism have, for example, been linked to the onset of mental and physical disorders and a declining health status <ref type="bibr">(Jokela et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">A. J. Wright & Jackson, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, not only mean-level and rank-order changes in personality traits can be practically relevant but also changes in the variance of personality traits are of practical relevance as they provide a complementary perspective on personality development.
When the variance of a personality trait is small, individuals are more similar to one another, leaving less room for the trait to explain differences in important life outcomes.
In contrast, greater variance increases the potential for the trait to predict who fares better or worse in domains such as health, work, or relationships.

In contrast to the rich empirical evidence on rank-order and mean-level changes in personality traits across the lifespan, variance changes have received comparably little attention (Mõttus et al., 2016 (Mõttus et al., , 2017)).
text.formatted: In contrast to the rich empirical evidence on rank-order and mean-level changes in personality traits across the lifespan, variance changes have received comparably little attention <ref type="bibr">(Mõttus et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Mõttus et al., , 2017))</ref>.

text.text: The variance of personality traits describes the extent of individual differences in a certain population.

Given that the concept of personality traits is based on the description of individual differences in thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, examining and explaining variance changes should be a core research target of personality science (Mõttus et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Given that the concept of personality traits is based on the description of individual differences in thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, examining and explaining variance changes should be a core research target of personality science <ref type="bibr">(Mõttus et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: As illustrated in Figure 1, changes in the variance of personality traits provide a unique perspective on personality development that is distinct from changes in the mean-levels and rank-orders of traits.
text.formatted: As illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, changes in the variance of personality traits provide a unique perspective on personality development that is distinct from changes in the mean-levels and rank-orders of traits.

text.text: Specifically, developmental changes in the variance of traits describe at the population level whether people become more different or more alike across the lifespan.

Modern theories of personality development emphasize that a person's age and the time interval between assessments are key factors moderating the extent of mean-level and rank-order change in personality traits (Bleidorn, 2024; Roberts & Nickel, 2017).
text.formatted: Modern theories of personality development emphasize that a person's age and the time interval between assessments are key factors moderating the extent of mean-level and rank-order change in personality traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bleidorn, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & Nickel, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, theoretical frameworks differ in the suggested mechanisms of personality development and their predictions about how age and time shape personality trajectories (Bleidorn et al., 2021; Specht et al., 2014).
text.formatted: However, theoretical frameworks differ in the suggested mechanisms of personality development and their predictions about how age and time shape personality trajectories <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bleidorn et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Specht et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: These theoretical distinctions extend to predictions about changes in trait variance over time.

Thus, studying how people's age and the time between assessments relate to changes in personality variance-alongside mean and rank-order changes-offers a more comprehensive evaluation of the premises of personality development theories and a deeper understanding of when and why individuals diverge or converge in their developmental pathways.

For example, a key principle of the Neo-Socioanalytic Theory of Personality (Caspi et al., 2005; Roberts & Nickel, 2017) states that people tend to select into environments that match their personality traits, and that these environments, in turn, reinforce the personality traits that led individuals to select into these environments in the first place.
text.formatted: For example, a key principle of the Neo-Socioanalytic Theory of Personality <ref type="bibr">(Caspi et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & Nickel, 2017)</ref> states that people tend to select into environments that match their personality traits, and that these environments, in turn, reinforce the personality traits that led individuals to select into these environments in the first place.

text.text: For example, a person with high levels in openness to experience may be more likely to engage in various stimulating activities (e.g., traveling around the world, visiting art exhibitions, or taking part in intellectual discussions), which may then, in turn, lead to further increases in their openness (Schwaba et al., 2018).
text.formatted: For example, a person with high levels in openness to experience may be more likely to engage in various stimulating activities (e.g., traveling around the world, visiting art exhibitions, or taking part in intellectual discussions), which may then, in turn, lead to further increases in their openness <ref type="bibr">(Schwaba et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This "Corresponsive Principle" thus implies that the variance of personality traits should increase over time and with older age because corresponsive life experiences tend to reinforce pre-existing individual differences (Mõttus et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This "Corresponsive Principle" thus implies that the variance of personality traits should increase over time and with older age because corresponsive life experiences tend to reinforce pre-existing individual differences <ref type="bibr">(Mõttus et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, according to the Five-Factor Theory (McCrae & Costa, 2008) personality trait development is almost exclusively driven by genetically shaped biological processes and should be largely completed by age 30 (Mõttus, 2017).
text.formatted: In contrast, according to the Five-Factor Theory <ref type="bibr">(McCrae & Costa, 2008)</ref> personality trait development is almost exclusively driven by genetically shaped biological processes and should be largely completed by age 30 <ref type="bibr">(Mõttus, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: As such, this theory implies that the mean levels, rank orders, and variance of personality traits should be highly stable in middle and old adulthood.

Although empirical research has shown that this expectation is not tenable for the mean levels and rank orders of personality traits (Bleidorn et al., 2022; Roberts, Walton, & Viechtbauer, 2006; Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000), it could still be the case that biologically driven personality development processes stabilize the variance of personality traits in adulthood.
text.formatted: Although empirical research has shown that this expectation is not tenable for the mean levels and rank orders of personality traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts, Walton, & Viechtbauer, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000)</ref>, it could still be the case that biologically driven personality development processes stabilize the variance of personality traits in adulthood.

text.text: For example, genetically predisposed set-points could counter-act potentially variance-increasing effects of corresponsive life experiences (Ormel et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For example, genetically predisposed set-points could counter-act potentially variance-increasing effects of corresponsive life experiences <ref type="bibr">(Ormel et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, another principle of the Neo-Socioanalytic Theory of Personality (Roberts & Nickel, 2017)-the Maturity Principle-suggests that people become more agreeable, more conscientious, and more emotionally stable as they age (Bleidorn, 2015; Schwaba et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Finally, another principle of the Neo-Socioanalytic Theory of Personality (Roberts & Nickel, 2017)-the Maturity Principle-suggests that people become more agreeable, more conscientious, and more emotionally stable as they age <ref type="bibr">(Bleidorn, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Schwaba et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This personality maturation has been explained by the investment in normative social roles in early adulthood, as described in the Social Investment Principle (Lodi-Smith & Roberts, 2007).
text.formatted: This personality maturation has been explained by the investment in normative social roles in early adulthood, as described in the Social Investment Principle <ref type="bibr">(Lodi-Smith & Roberts, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: To the extent that socialization processes shape personality traits (Denissen et al., 2019; Haehner, Krämer, Wright, et al., 2025; but see Asselmann & Specht, 2021), they may not only shift the mean levels of these traits but also reduce their variance, as individuals increasingly conform to social role demands and adopt socially acceptable behaviors (Mõttus et al., 2019).
text.formatted: To the extent that socialization processes shape personality traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Denissen et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Krämer, Wright, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">but see Asselmann & Specht, 2021)</ref>, they may not only shift the mean levels of these traits but also reduce their variance, as individuals increasingly conform to social role demands and adopt socially acceptable behaviors <ref type="bibr">(Mõttus et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In summary, theories of personality development have diverging implications regarding the development of personality trait variance across time and age.
At the same time, most theories do not include explicit statements about whether and how the variance of personality traits is expected to change across the lifespan.

As a result, scholars often differ in their interpretations of whether a certain personality development theory implies increases, decreases, or stability in personality trait variance (Bleidorn et al., 2021; McCrae, 1993; Mõttus et al., 2016 Mõttus et al., , 2017;; Roberts & Nickel, 2021).
text.formatted: As a result, scholars often differ in their interpretations of whether a certain personality development theory implies increases, decreases, or stability in personality trait variance <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bleidorn et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">McCrae, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mõttus et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mõttus et al., , 2017;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & Nickel, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The absence of clear theoretical predictions about the lifespan patterns of changes in trait variance is problematic, because an understanding of these changes is critical for a comprehensive description of lifespan personality trait development (Bleidorn, 2024; Mõttus et al., 2017 Mõttus et al., , 2019)).
text.formatted: The absence of clear theoretical predictions about the lifespan patterns of changes in trait variance is problematic, because an understanding of these changes is critical for a comprehensive description of lifespan personality trait development <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bleidorn, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mõttus et al., 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mõttus et al., , 2019))</ref>.

Other disciplines such as biology, economics, or sociology have rich histories in examining variance changes as a unique and informative phenomenon to better understand developing systems (Braumoeller, 2006; Gould, 1988; Killick et al., 2010; Malik, 2003; Mearns et al., 1997).
text.formatted: Other disciplines such as biology, economics, or sociology have rich histories in examining variance changes as a unique and informative phenomenon to better understand developing systems <ref type="bibr">(Braumoeller, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gould, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Killick et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Malik, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mearns et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: For example, economic research monitors variance changes in indicators like the gross domestic product to identify disruption phases and evaluate the effects of external shocks to the economic system (Amini et al., 2017; Braumoeller, 2006; French & Sichel, 1993).
text.formatted: For example, economic research monitors variance changes in indicators like the gross domestic product to identify disruption phases and evaluate the effects of external shocks to the economic system <ref type="bibr">(Amini et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Braumoeller, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">French & Sichel, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, climate research does not only investigate mean-level changes in temperature, ocean-levels, or rainfall but also climate-change induced changes in their variance (Killick et al., 2010; Shama, 2017; Thornton et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Similarly, climate research does not only investigate mean-level changes in temperature, ocean-levels, or rainfall but also climate-change induced changes in their variance <ref type="bibr">(Killick et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Shama, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Thornton et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Learning from these disciplines, considering variance changes in addition to meanlevel changes is critical to comprehensively describe the development of psychological characteristics, and, in doing so, constrain theories of lifespan development that need to explain the specifics of these change patters (Bleidorn, 2024).
text.formatted: Learning from these disciplines, considering variance changes in addition to meanlevel changes is critical to comprehensively describe the development of psychological characteristics, and, in doing so, constrain theories of lifespan development that need to explain the specifics of these change patters <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bleidorn, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: First, variance changes can reveal developmental dynamics that mean-level analyses obscure.

For example, increasing variance in psychological characteristics like beliefs, attitudes, or personality traits may help to identify disruptive life phases that may be overseen when examining mean-level changes only.
Second, studying variance changes also helps identify sensitive periods for intervention (Bleidorn et al., 2019; Haehner, Wright, & Bleidorn, 2024).
text.formatted: Second, studying variance changes also helps identify sensitive periods for intervention <ref type="bibr">(Bleidorn et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Wright, & Bleidorn, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: If the variance of a construct increases at certain life stages, this may suggest greater plasticity or openness to change-key windows when interventions might be particularly effective or when individuals are more responsive to environmental influences.
Conversely, periods of low variance might indicate stability or resistance to change, with different implications for intervention design.

Third, variance analyses can inform theories of person-environment transactions and developmental regulation by clarifying when and why individuals diverge or converge in their psychological characteristics (Bleidorn et al., 2020; Haehner, Wright, Krämer, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Third, variance analyses can inform theories of person-environment transactions and developmental regulation by clarifying when and why individuals diverge or converge in their psychological characteristics <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bleidorn et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Wright, Krämer, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Increases in personality trait variance may reflect differential exposure to life events, coping strategies, or goal prioritization, offering insight into the mechanisms that drive individual differences over time.
For example, during young adulthood, individuals tend to encounter vastly different educational, occupational, and relational contexts, which can lead to divergent developmental trajectories.
In such cases, rising variance may signal increasing differentiation in psychological outcomes due to unequal exposure to opportunities, stressors, or support systems.

Fourth, understanding variance changes can help contextualize existing work on mean-level changes in personality traits such that variance changes would inform us whether, for example, mean-level changes are driven by certain individuals having more extreme trait levels-just as it is part of every descriptive analysis to report mean values and variances together.

Finally, the variance of a construct is a characteristic of fundamental relevance for statistical modeling, including the prediction of important life outcomes or examining correlations with other variables.
In summary, changes in personality trait variance are of critical practical relevance.
Robust empirical evidence on changes in personality trait variance across time and age is thus needed to advance our understanding of personality development regarding this important phenomenon.
A handful of cross-sectional studies tested whether the variance of personality traits differed between age groups.

Using data from three different countries, Mõttus et al. (2016) found no systematic differences in the variance of personality traits between young adults (20-30 years) and middle-aged adults (50-60 years).
text.formatted: Using data from three different countries, <ref type="bibr">Mõttus et al. (2016)</ref> found no systematic differences in the variance of personality traits between young adults (20-30 years) and middle-aged adults (50-60 years).

text.text: Similarly, Soto et al.
(2011), Allemand et al. (2008), and Olaru et al. (2024) did not find systematic age group differences in the variance of the Big Five personality traits across different adult samples.

In contrast to these results, Allemand et al. (2007) found more variance in openness to experiences in middle-aged adults (42-46 years) than in older adults (60-64 years), whereas McCrae (1993) found that neuroticism had a higher variance in young age (21-49 years) compared to old age (50-96 years).
Finally, Mõttus et al. (2017) and Mõttus et al. (2019) found increases in personality trait variance from early childhood to early adolescence for agreeableness, conscientiousness, and neuroticism.

However, longitudinal studies are needed to fully understand changes in personality trait variance across time and age because they do not confound age effects and cohort effects and are less influenced by time-invariant confounding variables, including stable sample characteristics.
To the best of our knowledge, there are only two longitudinal studies that directly examined changes in personality trait variance.
However, these studies did not find changes in the variance of personality traits over time-neither over a 4-year (Allemand et al., 2007) nor over a 6-year period (Small et al., 2003).
text.formatted: However, these studies did not find changes in the variance of personality traits over time-neither over a 4-year (Allemand et al., 2007) nor over a 6-year period <ref type="bibr">(Small et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: In summary, empirical evidence on whether and how the variance of personality traits changes throughout the lifespan is limited and existing results are inconsistent.

The mixed pattern of evidence underlines the importance of a meta-analytic integration to draw a more precise picture of the lifespan trajectory of personality trait variance, examine potential moderators, and highlight existing gaps in this literature (see Mõttus et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The mixed pattern of evidence underlines the importance of a meta-analytic integration to draw a more precise picture of the lifespan trajectory of personality trait variance, examine potential moderators, and highlight existing gaps in this literature (see <ref type="bibr">Mõttus et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, such a meta-analytic integration is possible despite the fact that only few existing studies were explicitly designed to examine changes in the variance of personality traits, as long as the critical parameters -the variance (or standard deviation) of traits and sample size assessed at two or more measurement occasions over time -are available (Nakagawa et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Importantly, such a meta-analytic integration is possible despite the fact that only few existing studies were explicitly designed to examine changes in the variance of personality traits, as long as the critical parameters -the variance (or standard deviation) of traits and sample size assessed at two or more measurement occasions over time -are available <ref type="bibr">(Nakagawa et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: As such, we were able to reuse and extend existing meta-analytic databases of longitudinal studies of personality trait development (Bleidorn et al., 2022; Roberts, Walton, & Viechtbauer, 2006).
text.formatted: As such, we were able to reuse and extend existing meta-analytic databases of longitudinal studies of personality trait development <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts, Walton, & Viechtbauer, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond clarifying conflicting empirical findings, a meta-analytic perspective on changes in the variance of personality traits provides some unique opportunities.
First, no single empirical study is able to examine the entire lifespan.
Differences in existing research can at least partly be explained by focusing on different age groups.

Thus, by integrating findings across multiple studies with different age groups and time intervals between assessments, we can examine the effects of age and time on changes in personality trait variance across the lifespan.
Second, a meta-analytic aggregation of findings permits conclusions on the robustness and generalizability of changes in personality trait variance across samples, studies, and research approaches.

Third, and relatedly, a meta-analytic aggregation allows to examine further methodological moderators of changes in the variance of personality traits beyond time and age to begin to explain between-study heterogeneity.
Beyond age-and time-related differences, changes in the variance of personality traits may also depend on certain publication, sample, and measurement characteristics.

To better understand potential heterogeneity in the effect sizes, we explored the same moderators that have been tested in the meta-analyses on mean-level and rank-order changes of personality traits by Bleidorn et al. (2022).
text.formatted: To better understand potential heterogeneity in the effect sizes, we explored the same moderators that have been tested in the meta-analyses on mean-level and rank-order changes of personality traits by <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bleidorn et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, as primary research on the variance of personality traits is scarce, we had no specific hypotheses of how these additional, methodological moderators would be related to variance changes.
We examined the publication year as a potential moderator of changes in personality trait variance.
The reporting standards of longitudinal studies have changed over the last decades.

Due to these differences in reporting (e.g., regarding study attrition or assessment characteristics), the publication year may be associated with between-study heterogeneity in changes in personality trait variance.
We examined three sample characteristics (representativeness of the sample, gender composition, and region of data collection) as possible moderators of changes in personality trait variance.
First, we tested whether changes in personality trait variance differed between representative and non-representative samples.
In general, the variance of personality traits should be larger in representative samples as they are more heterogenous than, for example, non-representative student samples.
However, it is unclear whether the representativeness of a sample is related to variance changes in personality traits.

Second, although mean-level and rank-order changes in personality traits seem to be consistent across gender (Bleidorn et al., 2022), we explored whether changes in personality trait variance differed depending on the percentage of female participants in a sample.
text.formatted: Second, although mean-level and rank-order changes in personality traits seem to be consistent across gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref>, we explored whether changes in personality trait variance differed depending on the percentage of female participants in a sample.

text.text: Third, the majority of research has focused on personality development in Western societies, and comparatively little is known on personality traits in other regions such as Asia or Africa (Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2025; Thalmayer et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Third, the majority of research has focused on personality development in Western societies, and comparatively little is known on personality traits in other regions such as Asia or Africa <ref type="bibr">(Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Thalmayer et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: To better understand potential cultural differences in personality development, we explored whether the region of data collection was related to changes in personality trait variance.

Finally, we tested seven measurement characteristics as potential moderators of changes in personality trait variance (reliability, mode of assessment, broadness of the measure, maladaptation of the assessed trait, coding of the assessed trait, assessment of Big Five traits, mean-level changes).

First, as measurement error may attenuate assessments of trait variance, we examined whether the reliability of a personality trait measure was related to changes in the variance of personality traits.
Second, we examined whether the mode of assessment (self-report vs. other-report) was related to changes in personality trait variance.
Third, we explored potential differences between measures assessing broad trait domains and measures assessing personality traits on a facet level.
Fourth, we tested differences between measures assessing adaptive personality traits (e.g., agreeableness) and measures assessing maladaptive personality traits (e.g., disinhibition, aggression).
Fifth, we tested differences between scales in which high values are socially desirable and scales in which low values are socially desirable.

Sixth, we explored whether changes in the variance of personality traits differed between measures that were designed to assess the Big Five personality traits and measures that were not designed to assess the Big Five.
Seventh, we investigated whether changes in personality trait variance were associated with mean-level changes over the same time interval (Nakagawa et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Seventh, we investigated whether changes in personality trait variance were associated with mean-level changes over the same time interval <ref type="bibr">(Nakagawa et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, these moderator analyses allowed us to examine whether changes in personality trait variance are robust across these methodological characteristics or whether publication, sample, or assessment characteristics predict decreases or increases in personality trait variance across the lifespan.

Although the examination of variance changes in personality traits is of theoretical and practical importance, existing empirical research and theoretical discussions of this topic have been scarce (Mõttus, 2016; Mõttus et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Although the examination of variance changes in personality traits is of theoretical and practical importance, existing empirical research and theoretical discussions of this topic have been scarce <ref type="bibr">(Mõttus, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mõttus et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: To overcome this limitation, the present meta-analysis examined changes in personality traits variance across time and age by integrating data from existing longitudinal studies.
Furthermore, we explored whether other methodological moderators beyond age and time were related to changes in the personality trait variance.
To do this, we built on the works by Roberts et al. (2006) and Bleidorn et al. (2022) who meta-analytically integrated changes in the mean-levels of personality traits.
text.formatted: To do this, we built on the works by <ref type="bibr">Roberts et al. (2006)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bleidorn et al. (2022)</ref> who meta-analytically integrated changes in the mean-levels of personality traits.

text.text: Their metaanalytic datasets included the necessary information to examine changes in personality trait variance.

We extended these datasets by updating their literature searches to include more recent studies and to provide a comprehensive assessment of how the variance of personality traits change across the lifespan.
